costGuide.title: Mercedes M276 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a Mercedes M276 typically takes 12-16 hours at £65/hr (independent specialist rate) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes, as the 90-degree V6 layout requires careful access planning.
paragraphs: The final cost of a Mercedes M276 engine replacement is heavily influenced by whether the unit is naturally aspirated or biturbo, and the condition of the timing chain guides. Biturbo variants (.920, .960) carry a premium due to the complexity of the hot-vee turbo plumbing and intercoolers. Additionally, direct-injection variants often require intake valve carbon cleaning during the swap. failures.title: Mercedes M276 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Guide Wear
items.whatHappens: Early production M276 engines are susceptible to timing chain stretch and plastic guide wear. This manifests as a distinct metallic rattling noise on cold starts, followed by check engine lights indicating camshaft correlation faults. If ignored, the chain can jump teeth, leading to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, replacing the timing chain kit, tensioners, and guides is viable, though it is a labour-intensive job requiring significant front-end strip-down. If internal damage has already occurred, a full Mercedes M276 engine replacement is the only reliable solution.

items.title: Intake Valve Carbon Buildup (Direct Injection Variants)
items.whatHappens: On M276 variants equipped with direct injection, fuel is sprayed directly into the cylinder, bypassing the intake valves. This eliminates the "washing" effect of port injection, allowing oil vapours from the PCV system to accumulate and form hard carbon deposits on the intake valves and ports. This leads to rough idle, misfires, and reduced power.
items.repairVsReplace: Carbon buildup is addressed via walnut blasting or chemical cleaning of the intake tract, not engine replacement. However, severe neglect combined with timing chain issues can compound repair costs, making a reconditioned swap more economical than piecemeal repairs.

items.title: Oil Leaks from Gaskets and Seals
items.whatHappens: The M276 is prone to oil leaks from the valve cover gaskets, oil cooler seals, and camshaft adjuster solenoids. Over time, heat cycles cause these rubber components to harden and crack, leading to oil loss and a persistent burning oil smell in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: Gasket and seal replacement is a standard, relatively inexpensive preventative repair. However, if severe oil starvation has occurred due to ignored leaks, a reconditioned engine swap becomes the most economical long-term fix.

variants.title: M276 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The M276 family covers several raw sub-codes that share the same core 90-degree V6 architecture but differ by displacement, forced induction, and calibration. Identifying your exact sub-code is critical, as components like the turbochargers, intake manifold, ECU, and engine mounts are not universally interchangeable. - Fitted to: Mercedes E-Class (W213 E400), CLS (C218/C257 CLS400) - Key technical difference: Features twin turbochargers mounted in the "hot-vee" between the cylinder banks, paired with direct injection for high torque output. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain pattern; hot-vee turbo plumbing adds complexity to oil leak diagnostics. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with naturally aspirated variants; the ECU, wiring loom, exhaust manifolds, and cooling systems differ significantly. - Fitted to: Mercedes E-Class (W213 E350), Mercedes ML (W164 ML350), Mercedes GL (X166 GL350) - Key technical difference: The mid-range 3.5-litre naturally aspirated variant, featuring port injection (or early direct injection in some markets) and a conventional intake layout. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain and oil leak patterns; carbon buildup is less severe than on later direct-injection-only models. - Interchange note: Physically similar to the 3.0L biturbo but requires the correct ECU calibration and specific exhaust routing to run safely. - Fitted to: Mercedes E-Class (W213 E300), Mercedes S-Class (W221/W222 S300 Hybrid) - Key technical difference: The entry-level 3.0-litre variant, often paired with a mild-hybrid system (e.g., S300 BlueHYBRID) to improve urban fuel economy. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain pattern; hybrid integration requires specific ECU and electrical compatibility. - Interchange note: Cannot be swapped with higher-output 3.5L or biturbo units without extensive ECU, wiring, and hybrid system modifications. - Fitted to: Mercedes GLE (W166 GLE400), CLS (C218/C257 CLS400) - Key technical difference: The high-output 3.5-litre biturbo variant, featuring revised turbochargers and updated engine calibration for increased torque in heavier SUV applications. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain pattern; higher thermal loads on SUV applications can accelerate oil seal degradation if service intervals are extended.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Mercedes M276 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Mercedes M276 is only advisable for lower-mileage host vehicles and *only* if accompanied by documented, stamped service history proving the timing chain and guides have been inspected or replaced. Without this history, the risk of inheriting the same catastrophic chain-jump issues is unacceptably high.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the most recommended route for the M276. A proper reconditioned unit will include brand-new timing chain components, refreshed valve cover and oil cooler gaskets, and a cleaned intake tract to address direct-injection carbon buildup, directly addressing the engine's known weak points out of the box.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if your original M276 suffered a jumped timing chain that damaged the cylinder head, valves, or pistons. A specialist rebuild will machine the block, fit updated timing components, and ensure all oil galleries are clear of debris from the failed chain.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing a replacement is only half the job. Our network provides full supply and fit services, ensuring the engine is installed by Mercedes-specialist technicians with a nationwide warranty backing both the labour and the unit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For core hosts like the W213 E-Class, W166 GLE, and W222 S-Class, current UK market values typically sit between £8,000 and £35,000 . With a reconditioned M276 replacement costing from £3,800 (plus fitting), the repair cost generally represents 20-40% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable and a safe investment for well-maintained examples.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M276 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure patterns for the M276 are timing chain stretch/guide wear and intake valve carbon buildup on direct-injection variants. Early warning signs include a metallic rattle on cold starts and camshaft correlation fault codes, while carbon buildup manifests as a rough idle, misfires, and reduced power, often requiring walnut blasting to resolve.

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M276 engine?
items.answer: The M276 is fitted to Mercedes-Benz core models from 2011 to 2020, including the E-Class (W213), CLS (C218/C257), GLE (W166), and S-Class (W221/W222). It powers badges ranging from the E300 and E350 to the GLE400 and S350, and you should always verify your exact sub-code via registration lookup before ordering parts.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M276 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M276 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the well-documented timing chain and carbon buildup risks. Used units carry a high probability of inheriting the same latent wear unless accompanied by stamped proof of a full chain kit replacement, whereas a proper reconditioned M276 includes new timing chain components, refreshed gaskets, and a cleaned intake tract as standard.

items.question: What is the difference between the M276.920, M276.940, M276.950, and M276.960?
items.answer: The M276.920 is a 3.0L biturbo, the M276.940 is a 3.5L naturally aspirated, the M276.950 is a 3.0L naturally aspirated (often hybrid), and the M276.960 is a 3.5L biturbo. While they share the same core 90-degree V6 architecture, they differ in forced induction, displacement, and ECU calibration, meaning fitting the wrong variant will result in severe ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities.
